title: B.C. aboriginals mourn woman killed by RCMP
article: Nine days ago, native elders on Cormorant Island held a ceremony to cleanse the community of a past that included residential-school abuse. They hoped it would signal positive times ahead.
Tonight, they will gather to seek answers to another tragedy, the shooting death of a mother by a Mountie in the aboriginal community of Whe-La-La-U.
Lorraine Jacobson, 40, was killed Friday night while her 10-year-old daughter was at home.

Her death has native leaders wondering how the event could have occurred, especially after so much talk of healing and reconciliation among aboriginals and non-natives living on Cormorant Island, off the northeast coast of Vancouver Island.
"This shooting has strained relations," said Lawrence Ambers, band administrator for the Namgis First Nation, whose reserve surrounds Whe-La-La-U.
RCMP officials said yesterday that an officer was responding to a complaint of a domestic disturbance at Ms. Jacobson's home.
The constable who shot Ms. Jacobson with a 9 mm handgun had to think fast because she was headed toward him with a large butcher knife, the RCMP said.

Native leaders identified the officer as Constable Russ Chanin, who is part of a four-person detachment in Alert Bay, also on Cormorant Island. He is an eight-year veteran with two years' experience in Alert Bay, and is now off duty with pay and receiving crisis counselling.
There are conflicting accounts of how many times Constable Chanin warned Ms. Jacobson to drop the knife. Police say there were several warnings; one witness said there was only one.
Ms. Jacobson collapsed after being shot once in the chest.
Two men were in her townhouse at the time, and so was her daughter, Summer. Her 11-year-old son, Lance, was at a neighbour's home.
Ms. Jacobson was taken to Alert Bay Hospital in a police cruiser. She was pronounced dead on arrival.
Mr. Ambers said tonight's meeting at the Namgis recreation centre with RCMP representatives and non-natives should serve as a way for aboriginals to overcome the shock of how Ms. Jacobson died.

"There's a lot of anger and extremely high tension in our community. People just don't understand why this had to happen," he said. "This is an unfortunate, tragic event for us. We need to go through a community healing process. We've invited the entire island to come to the meeting."
Ms. Jacobson, who also went by the name Lorraine Moon, is from the Squamish Nation but had roots in the Alert Bay area.

RCMP Sergeant Lee Omilusik said a coroner's inquest will be held into the killing and the RCMP's major-crime unit from Courtenay on Vancouver Island has been called in to conduct an internal investigation.

"Our training is such that if you're confronted with a situation where you have no other option but to use deadly force, then we are trained to shoot centre mass -- the centre of the victim," said Sgt. Omilusik, a police spokesman from Port Alberni on Vancouver Island. "You have a split-second decision to make."
